slides.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
content: Back-of-the-envelope estimation is a quick approximate calculation to evaluate system scale and feasibility
Used to estimate capacity, traffic, and storage before detailed system design
Helps validate architecture decisions early in interviews
Focus is on logical reasoning and correct order of magnitude, not exact precision
Always state assumptions clearly and use proper units

slides.title: Power of Two (Storage Basics)
content: Storage calculations are based on binary powers such as 2^10, 2^20, 2^30
1 KB ≈ 10^3 bytes, 1 MB ≈ 10^6 bytes, 1 GB ≈ 10^9 bytes
1 TB ≈ 10^12 bytes and 1 PB ≈ 10^15 bytes
1 byte equals 8 bits and one ASCII character is approximately 1 byte
Important for estimating storage, memory usage, and bandwidth

slides.title: Latency Basics
content: Latency represents the time delay between request and response
CPU cache is fastest, followed by RAM, disk, and then network
Cross-region network calls are the slowest and most expensive
Memory access is faster than disk and network operations
System design should minimize disk access and network calls

slides.title: Availability and Nines
content: Availability is the percentage of time a system remains operational
99% availability means about 3.6 days downtime per year
99.9% gives around 8.7 hours downtime per year
99.99% gives around 52 minutes downtime per year
Higher availability requires more redundancy and increases system cost

slides.title: Core Estimation Metrics
content: QPS means queries per second and is calculated as total requests per day divided by 86400
Peak QPS is typically estimated as twice the average QPS
Storage estimation depends on size per item, number of items, and retention period
Bandwidth is calculated as QPS multiplied by response size
Number of servers is calculated using peak QPS divided by capacity per server with buffer

slides.title: Estimation Flow Pattern
content: Start by writing assumptions clearly before calculations
Estimate number of daily active users
Calculate total actions or requests per day
Compute average QPS and then peak QPS
Estimate storage requirements and long-term growth
Follow a structured approach to avoid missing steps

slides.title: Estimation Best Practices
content: Always state assumptions before solving
Use rounded numbers for easier calculations
Label all units clearly such as bytes, seconds, or requests
Focus on order of magnitude instead of exact values
Avoid mixing bits and bytes and do not ignore peak traffic

slides.title: Important Terms
content: Assumption is an estimated input used when exact data is unavailable
Order of magnitude represents the scale like thousands or millions
Feasibility checks whether the system design can work at scale
Latency is the delay between request and response
Throughput is the amount of work processed per unit time such as QPS
Bandwidth is the amount of data transferred per second

slides.title: QPS Estimation Example
content: Daily active users are calculated from total users and activity percentage
Total requests per day equals users multiplied by actions per user
Average QPS is calculated by dividing total requests by seconds in a day
Peak QPS is approximately twice the average QPS
Used to estimate system load and required infrastructure

slides.title: Storage Estimation Example
content: Calculate number of items generated per day based on user activity
Multiply items by size per item to get daily storage
Convert units from MB to GB or TB for clarity
Multiply daily storage by retention period to estimate long-term storage
Helps design storage systems for large-scale applications
